Well, hello there, doctor. Thank you for fitting me in. As for what brings me in... well, I’ve been retired for a few years now, and to keep myself busy and out of the house, I spend a good chunk of my time down at the local art museum. It’s a wonderful place, really, lots of good people. But lately, well, I guess it’s been happening for a while, but it’s getting to be a real bother and I figured I should talk to someone about it. 

See, people at the museum will be talking right to me—like, just the other day, we were trying to get things organized for the next art walk we do. And one of the folks there was giving me the rundown on the schedule and where we needed to set things up. And I’m looking right at them, you know, making eye contact, nodding along, trying my absolute best to pay attention. But then... I don't know, I just suddenly realize I completely missed the middle of what they said. It's like my brain just tuned out for a solid thirty seconds. I hear the beginning, I hear the end, but the middle is just gone. 

And it’s so embarrassing, it really is, because I’m standing right there, looking right into their eyes, and I have to stop them and ask them to run it by me again. And I hate doing that. I really do. It makes me feel like I’m being rude or like I don't care about what they have to say, which isn't true at all! I want to hear them, I just... the words just slip right past me even when I'm staring right at their face. I just don't understand why I can't seem to hold onto a simple conversation without needing a rewind, and it's happening enough now that I'm just getting frustrated with myself.

And I’m looking right at them, you know, making eye contact, nodding along, trying my absolute best to pay attention. But then... I don't know, I just suddenly realize I completely missed the middle of what they said. It's like my brain just tuned out for a solid thirty seconds. I hear the beginning, I hear the end, but the middle is just gone. \n\nAnd it’s so embarrassing, it really is, because I’m standing right there, looking right into their eyes, and I have to stop them and ask them to run it by me again. And I hate doing that. I really do. It makes me feel like I’m being rude or like I don't care about what they have to say, which isn't true at all! I want to hear them, I just... the words just slip right past me even when I'm staring right at their face. I just don't understand why I can't seem to hold onto a simple conversation without needing a rewind, and it's happening enough now that I'm just getting frustrated with myself.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any other changes in your thinking or memory lately, like forgetting things more often or feeling confused about time or places?\n\nPatient: Well, you know, I’ve actually asked myself that very same question. When you get to be my age—I'm 63, you know—you start to wonder if maybe the old memory bank is starting to rust a little bit. You hear stories about folks getting confused or forgetting their own phone numbers, or getting lost on their own street, and it terrifies you, it really does. But honestly? No. I haven’t noticed anything like that at all. My memory itself seems to be as sharp as a tack, thank goodness. \n\nFor instance, I can tell you the exact dates of every rotating exhibit we've had at the museum for the last three years, and I know all the names of the regular patrons who come in on Thursday mornings. Just this past weekend, I was telling my neighbor, Bill—he lives two doors down, got this beautiful golden retriever that always digs up my petunias, but that's a whole other story—anyway, I was telling him about a documentary I watched on the History Channel, and I remembered all the dates and the historical figures without missing a beat. So the information is definitely staying in my head once it actually gets in there! \n\nAnd as for getting confused about time or places, no, definitely not. I drive myself everywhere, take the same route down Elm Street to get to the museum, never get turned around or anything like that. I always know exactly what day it is, mostly because I keep a very strict routine since I retired from the workforce. Tuesday is trash day, Thursday is my morning shift at the information desk, Sunday is church... so I'm very anchored, you might say. \n\nIt’s really just that specific thing where I'm listening to someone and the words just sort of... evaporate while they're speaking. I’d say, 'Oh, I missed what you said because I was distracted by my stomach rumbling.' Or if there was a loud noise, like a siren going by outside the museum. We do get a fair amount of ambulances going down Elm Street because the county hospital is just two miles north of us, so you hear them quite a bit. \n\nBut no, it’s not like that at all. Just completely empty. \n\nOne second I'm listening to our coordinator, Susan—she's a lovely woman, been running the volunteer program for about ten years now, always wears these very colorful scarves—one second I'm listening to her talk about the new impressionist exhibit we're getting, and the next second, I realize I haven't processed a single word she said for a whole minute. And I try to search my brain, you know, to figure out where I went, what I was thinking about instead, and there's just nothing there. No sudden thoughts pulling me away, no distractions, just a big blank space where her words were supposed to go. Oh, no, no, I’m definitely still right there in the room. I haven't gone anywhere, so to speak. I know exactly where I am and what's going on around me. 

Like with Susan, for example, when she’s talking to me and my brain does that little static thing, I can still see her perfectly fine. I can see her waving her hands—she talks with her hands a lot, you see. Her husband is Italian, lovely man named Marco, makes a fantastic lasagna, and she always jokes that she picked up the hand-waving habit from his side of the family. So I can see her doing that, and I can feel the hard floor under my shoes. We have these beautiful polished marble floors in the main lobby of the museum, gorgeous to look at but very, very hard on the knees and lower back if you stand on them too long. That's actually why I had to go and buy these special orthopedic inserts from the pharmacy down on 4th street. They have the little gel pads in the heels? Highly recommend them, by the way, if you're on your feet all day in the clinic here. 

But anyway, my point is, I can feel my feet on the floor, I can see the dust motes catching the light from the big bay windows, I can hear the hum of the air conditioner kicking on. I am completely, one hundred percent aware of my surroundings. It’s not like I pass out or fall asleep with my eyes open or anything scary like that. I read an article in a magazine once about people who have these little... I don't know, mini-seizures or something, where they just completely blank out and don't even know time passed. It's definitely not that. I know time is passing. 

I know I'm standing there, and I know she's talking to me. I can even hear the actual sound of her voice making noise. It's just... the meaning of the words just doesn't connect in my head. It's like she suddenly switched to speaking Greek halfway through the sentence. I’m just standing there, looking right at her, nodding my head like a fool, fully aware that I am nodding and fully aware that she is speaking, but the actual content? The instructions about the painting or the schedule? Just gone. Just noise. And I'm just waiting for her to finish her sentence so I can do the whole, "I'm so sorry, my mind wandered, could you repeat that?" routine. Which, like I said, is just getting so incredibly old. Because I am right there, I really am, the words just aren't clicking.

So, no, no confusion or real memory loss, just that frustrating tuning-out business when people are talking to me.\n\nDoctor: When you find yourself tuning out during conversations, are you aware of anything else going on in your mind or around you at that moment, like distractions or sudden thoughts pulling your attention away?\n\nPatient: You know, that’s the strangest part of the whole thing, it really is. If I were sitting there daydreaming about what I was going to have for lunch—which, by the way, I usually just have a simple turkey sandwich, nothing fancy, maybe a little bit of that spicy mustard my daughter brought me from her trip to upstate New York last fall—but if I was thinking about that, well, then it would make sense, wouldn't it? I’m not thinking about my grocery list, I’m not looking over the person's shoulder at a painting, I'm not distracted by anything I can actually put my finger on. It’s more like... well, it’s like my brain just goes to static. Just completely empty. \n\nOne second I'm listening to our coordinator, Susan—she's a lovely woman, been running the volunteer program for about ten years now, always wears these very colorful scarves—one second I'm listening to her talk about the new impressionist exhibit we're getting, and the next second, I realize I haven't processed a single word she said for a whole minute. And I try to search my brain, you know, to figure out where I went, what I was thinking about instead, and there's just nothing there. No sudden thoughts pulling me away, no distractions, just a big blank space where her words were supposed to go. But how do you stop yourself from thinking about absolutely nothing at all?\n\nDoctor: During these moments when your brain feels like it goes to static, do you lose awareness of what’s happening around you, or do you remain aware but just unable to process the words?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, no, I’m definitely still right there in the room. I haven't gone anywhere, so to speak. I know exactly where I am and what's going on around me. \n\nLike with Susan, for example, when she’s talking to me and my brain does that little static thing, I can still see her perfectly fine. Highly recommend them, by the way, if you're on your feet all day in the clinic here. \n\nBut anyway, my point is, I can feel my feet on the floor, I can see the dust motes catching the light from the big bay windows, I can hear the hum of the air conditioner kicking on. I am completely, one hundred percent aware of my surroundings. It’s not like I pass out or fall asleep with my eyes open or anything scary like that. I read an article in a magazine once about people who have these little... I don't know, mini-seizures or something, where they just completely blank out and don't even know time passed. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, now that you mention it, reading can be a bit of a chore sometimes. It's funny you bring that up, because I was just dealing with this the other day. 

Susan—the one I mentioned earlier, from the museum—she prints out these informational packets for us volunteers every time a new exhibit rotates in. They're usually, oh, I don't know, maybe ten or twelve pages long, stapled in the top left corner. She uses this very nice, heavy stock paper, but she insists on using a font that I swear is a size ten. I've told her, 'Susan, we're not spring chickens here, maybe bump it up to a twelve,' but she says it saves on the museum's printing budget, which I suppose I understand. 

But anyway, I'll sit down in my armchair at home—the green one by the front window, it gets the absolute best light in the late afternoons—with one of these gallery packets or a set of notes she's given us. And I start out just fine. I really do. I read the first paragraph, maybe the second, and I'm taking it all in, learning about the Bronze Age or whatever it happens to be that month. 

But then, after just a few minutes... it's the strangest thing. My eyes are still moving over the page, going line by line, left to right, just like they're supposed to. But my mind? It has completely wandered off. I'll be looking right at the words, but my brain is suddenly miles away, thinking about what I'm going to make for dinner, or wondering if I remembered to put the recycling bin out on the curb—pickup is Thursday mornings, you see, and the truck comes awfully early, usually right when I'm pouring my coffee. 

And then I'll suddenly realize I'm at the bottom of the page, and I haven't absorbed a single piece of information from the last three paragraphs. It's just like the listening thing, but with reading! My eyes did the work, but nobody was home to receive the mail, so to speak. So I have to go back up and read the exact same part all over again. Sometimes I have to read the same paragraph three or four times before it actually sticks in my head. 

As for television, well, I watch my evening news, like I said, and maybe a documentary here and there on the history channel, but I usually end up fiddling with a crossword puzzle while it's on because I just can't just sit and stare at the screen. Though, honestly, even with the crosswords, I'll stare at a clue for a 'five-letter word for boat' and the next thing I know I'm daydreaming about a fishing trip I took to Lake Michigan back in nineteen ninety-eight. Beautiful lake, by the way, though the wind coming off it will chill you right to the bone. But yes, I suppose keeping my attention locked on one thing for a long stretch, like a book or those gallery notes, is definitely a bit of a struggle.

Well, it wasn't exactly a sudden overnight thing, like waking up with a sore throat or a stiff neck, but I can tell you exactly when it really started becoming a noticeable issue. It’s been right about two years and four months now. I know the timeline so specifically because, well... it was right after my dear friend Arthur passed away. 

Arthur and I, we were quite the pair at the museum. We started volunteering there together back in... oh, it must have been two thousand and fifteen, maybe sixteen. He was such a wonderful fellow, always had a joke ready for the security guards, always wore these brightly colored bowties. But he had a bad heart, you see, and he passed away quite suddenly. It was a terrible time, just an awful shock to all of us. 

Anyway, Arthur was the official museum liaison for our volunteer group. He handled all the important paperwork, the scheduling with the local schools, making sure everyone had their gallery packets and knew where they were supposed to stand when the big tours came through. He kept everything perfectly organized in this giant red binder he carried around. But when he died, well, there was a big gap, and Susan asked me to step up. So I took over the museum liaison duties all by myself. And let me tell you, it is a tremendous amount of responsibility for one person to manage! 

And that is exactly when this whole... mind going blank business really started causing trouble for me. Because suddenly, I didn't have Arthur there to tap me on the shoulder if I spaced out during a meeting, and I had to read every single page of those informational packets myself to prepare the other volunteers. Before he passed, if my mind took a little walk while we were reading up on the new exhibits, Arthur would just fill me in on whatever I missed. He'd say, "Don't worry, I've got the important bits right here." But taking it all on by myself these last two years and four months... that's when it became glaringly obvious that my brain was taking these little detours. So I suppose my mind might have always wandered a little bit, but the trouble of it—the real, noticeable trouble—started exactly when I had to take over for Arthur.

Oh, no, absolutely not. I can honestly say I’ve never had a day like that. Goodness, if I didn't enjoy my time with Marmalade or my afternoons at the museum, I don't know what I'd do with myself!

Just completely empty. \n\nOne second I'm listening to our coordinator, Susan—she's a lovely woman, been running the volunteer program for about ten years now, always wears these very colorful scarves—one second I'm listening to her talk about the new impressionist exhibit we're getting, and the next second, I realize I haven't processed a single word she said for a whole minute. And I try to search my brain, you know, to figure out where I went, what I was thinking about instead, and there's just nothing there. No sudden thoughts pulling me away, no distractions, just a big blank space where her words were supposed to go. It’s incredibly frustrating because if I knew what was distracting me, maybe I could fix it, you know? I could tell myself to stop thinking about the lawn or the groceries. But how do you stop yourself from thinking about absolutely nothing at all?\n\nDoctor: During these moments when your brain feels like it goes to static, do you lose awareness of what’s happening around you, or do you remain aware but just unable to process the words?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, no, I’m definitely still right there in the room. I haven't gone anywhere, so to speak. I know exactly where I am and what's going on around me. \n\nLike with Susan, for example, when she’s talking to me and my brain does that little static thing, I can still see her perfectly fine. I can see her waving her hands—she talks with her hands a lot, you see. Her husband is Italian, lovely man named Marco, makes a fantastic lasagna, and she always jokes that she picked up the hand-waving habit from his side of the family. So I can see her doing that, and I can feel the hard floor under my shoes. We have these beautiful polished marble floors in the main lobby of the museum, gorgeous to look at but very, very hard on the knees and lower back if you stand on them too long. That's actually why I had to go and buy these special orthopedic inserts from the pharmacy down on 4th street. They have the little gel pads in the heels? Highly recommend them, by the way, if you're on your feet all day in the clinic here. \n\nBut anyway, my point is, I can feel my feet on the floor, I can see the dust motes catching the light from the big bay windows, I can hear the hum of the air conditioner kicking on. I am completely, one hundred percent aware of my surroundings. It’s not like I pass out or fall asleep with my eyes open or anything scary like that. I read an article in a magazine once about people who have these little... I don't know, mini-seizures or something, where they just completely blank out and don't even know time passed. He'd say, \"Don't worry, I've got the important bits right here.\" But taking it all on by myself these last two years and four months... that's when it became glaringly obvious that my brain was taking these little detours. So I suppose my mind might have always wandered a little bit, but the trouble of it—the real, noticeable trouble—started exactly when I had to take over for Arthur.\n\nDoctor: During the times when your mind goes blank, do you ever experience any strange or unwanted thoughts, mental images, or a sense that things are not real?\n\nPatient: Oh, heavens no, nothing like that. When you say strange or unwanted thoughts, I think of, oh, I don't know, those science fiction programs or something terribly dramatic. No, my thoughts are completely ordinary. Almost painfully boring, if I'm being entirely honest with you! \n\nWhen my mind takes its little walks, it's always to very everyday, mundane places. Like I mentioned before, it's the recycling, or what I'm having for supper. Just yesterday, for instance, I was supposed to be reading up on a new pottery exhibit—Mesopotamian, I believe, though don't quote me on that, Susan just handed us the packet on Tuesday—and my mind wandered right off to Marmalade's food situation. She’s gotten terribly picky in her old age, you see. She used to eat the dry kibble right out of the bag without a fuss, but now she turns her nose up at absolutely anything that isn't the salmon paté. And wouldn't you know it, the grocery store over on Main Street just rearranged their aisles last month, so the cat food is completely on the other side of the store now, right next to the baking supplies, which makes no sense at all to me. \n\nSo, no, there are no strange mental images or anything unwanted. It's just a matter of my attention being at the grocery store with the salmon paté instead of on the piece of paper right in front of my nose. Well, you know, once I actually realize I’ve drifted off, it’s really no trouble at all to get back on track. I don't feel like I have to heave and push to get my focus back, it just... snaps right back into place. 

Take the newspaper, for example. Like I was saying, I read the physical paper every morning in my green armchair. Let's say I'm reading an article about the town council—they've been going on and on for weeks in the local section about the zoning permits for that new strip mall over on Route 7, which, frankly, is going to make the traffic just absolutely unbearable during the evening rush, they never think these things through—and right in the middle of a paragraph, my mind just decides to wander off. I'll start wondering if I bought enough of Marmalade's salmon paté at the grocery store on Tuesday, or if I need to make a special trip to the pet shop. 

Now, the tricky part is just *noticing* that I've stopped reading. I might sit there staring at the exact same picture of the mayor for five minutes without absorbing a thing! But the very second I think to myself, "Oh, goodness, I'm not reading a word of this," I just blink, look down at the page, and I'm right back in it. I just find the last sentence I actually remember and off I go again. It doesn't take any special effort.

It’s the exact same thing when I'm talking to Susan at the museum. If she's telling me about the new schedule for the third-grade school tours, and I start thinking about whether I remembered to leave the porch light on for the mail carrier... well, the moment I realize I've tuned her out, I just say, "Oh, I'm so sorry Susan, my mind took a little detour there, what was that last part?" And I'm instantly right back in the conversation with her. 

It never feels like hard work. It's not like trying to push a heavy wheelbarrow up a steep hill—which I actually did try to do last spring when I was helping Mr. Henderson with his garden mulch, because his grandson was supposed to come help but never showed up, and let me tell you, my lower back was complaining about that for a solid week, I had to use the heating pad every single night while I watched Jeopardy. But no, pulling my attention back isn't like heavy lifting at all. It just pops right back to the present the moment I realize it went missing in the first place.

I want to hear them, I just... the words just slip right past me even when I'm staring right at their face. I just don't understand why I can't seem to hold onto a simple conversation without needing a rewind, and it's happening enough now that I'm just getting frustrated with myself.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any other changes in your thinking or memory lately, like forgetting things more often or feeling confused about time or places?\n\nPatient: Well, you know, I’ve actually asked myself that very same question. When you get to be my age—I'm 63, you know—you start to wonder if maybe the old memory bank is starting to rust a little bit. You hear stories about folks getting confused or forgetting their own phone numbers, or getting lost on their own street, and it terrifies you, it really does. But honestly? No. I haven’t noticed anything like that at all. My memory itself seems to be as sharp as a tack, thank goodness. \n\nFor instance, I can tell you the exact dates of every rotating exhibit we've had at the museum for the last three years, and I know all the names of the regular patrons who come in on Thursday mornings. So the information is definitely staying in my head once it actually gets in there! \n\nAnd as for getting confused about time or places, no, definitely not. I drive myself everywhere, take the same route down Elm Street to get to the museum, never get turned around or anything like that. I always know exactly what day it is, mostly because I keep a very strict routine since I retired from the workforce. Tuesday is trash day, Thursday is my morning shift at the information desk, Sunday is church... so I'm very anchored, you might say. \n\nIt’s really just that specific thing where I'm listening to someone and the words just sort of... evaporate while they're speaking. But once I actually catch what they're saying, or if I read it on a piece of paper, I remember it just fine! So, no, no confusion or real memory loss, just that frustrating tuning-out business when people are talking to me.\n\nDoctor: When you find yourself tuning out during conversations, are you aware of anything else going on in your mind or around you at that moment, like distractions or sudden thoughts pulling your attention away?\n\nPatient: You know, that’s the strangest part of the whole thing, it really is. If I were sitting there daydreaming about what I was going to have for lunch—which, by the way, I usually just have a simple turkey sandwich, nothing fancy, maybe a little bit of that spicy mustard my daughter brought me from her trip to upstate New York last fall—but if I was thinking about that, well, then it would make sense, wouldn't it? I’d say, 'Oh, I missed what you said because I was distracted by my stomach rumbling.' Or if there was a loud noise, like a siren going by outside the museum. We do get a fair amount of ambulances going down Elm Street because the county hospital is just two miles north of us, so you hear them quite a bit. \n\nBut no, it’s not like that at all. I’m not thinking about my grocery list, I’m not looking over the person's shoulder at a painting, I'm not distracted by anything I can actually put my finger on. It’s more like... well, it’s like my brain just goes to static. Just completely empty. \n\nOne second I'm listening to our coordinator, Susan—she's a lovely woman, been running the volunteer program for about ten years now, always wears these very colorful scarves—one second I'm listening to her talk about the new impressionist exhibit we're getting, and the next second, I realize I haven't processed a single word she said for a whole minute. And I try to search my brain, you know, to figure out where I went, what I was thinking about instead, and there's just nothing there. No sudden thoughts pulling me away, no distractions, just a big blank space where her words were supposed to go. It’s incredibly frustrating because if I knew what was distracting me, maybe I could fix it, you know? I could tell myself to stop thinking about the lawn or the groceries. But how do you stop yourself from thinking about absolutely nothing at all?\n\nDoctor: During these moments when your brain feels like it goes to static, do you lose awareness of what’s happening around you, or do you remain aware but just unable to process the words?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, no, I’m definitely still right there in the room. I haven't gone anywhere, so to speak. I know exactly where I am and what's going on around me. \n\nLike with Susan, for example, when she’s talking to me and my brain does that little static thing, I can still see her perfectly fine. I can see her waving her hands—she talks with her hands a lot, you see. Her husband is Italian, lovely man named Marco, makes a fantastic lasagna, and she always jokes that she picked up the hand-waving habit from his side of the family. So I can see her doing that, and I can feel the hard floor under my shoes. We have these beautiful polished marble floors in the main lobby of the museum, gorgeous to look at but very, very hard on the knees and lower back if you stand on them too long. That's actually why I had to go and buy these special orthopedic inserts from the pharmacy down on 4th street. They have the little gel pads in the heels? Highly recommend them, by the way, if you're on your feet all day in the clinic here. \n\nBut anyway, my point is, I can feel my feet on the floor, I can see the dust motes catching the light from the big bay windows, I can hear the hum of the air conditioner kicking on. I am completely, one hundred percent aware of my surroundings. It’s not like I pass out or fall asleep with my eyes open or anything scary like that. I read an article in a magazine once about people who have these little... I don't know, mini-seizures or something, where they just completely blank out and don't even know time passed. I’m just standing there, looking right at her, nodding my head like a fool, fully aware that I am nodding and fully aware that she is speaking, but the actual content? The instructions about the painting or the schedule? Just gone. Just noise. And I'm just waiting for her to finish her sentence so I can do the whole, \"I'm so sorry, my mind wandered, could you repeat that?\" routine. Which, like I said, is just getting so incredibly old. Because I am right there, I really am, the words just aren't clicking.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced any loss of awareness, jerking movements, or difficulty moving parts of your body during or right after these episodes?\n\nPatient: Oh, heavens no. My body works just fine—well, you know, as fine as you can expect for a sixty-three-year-old! I mean, sure, I get a little stiffness in my left knee when the weather turns cold. I don't freeze up like a statue where I can't move my legs, either. I can walk, I can turn my head, I can shift my weight from one foot to the other without any trouble at all. \n\nI actually know a fellow, Richard, from my old bowling league—I don't bowl anymore because of my shoulder, but I still go down to the alley on Wednesdays to keep score and socialize, they serve a surprisingly good chili dog there—anyway, Richard had a mild stroke a few years back, and he said his arm just stopped working out of nowhere. Just hung there like a wet noodle. It was terrifying for him, just awful. But I don't experience anything even remotely close to that. My arms and legs do exactly what I tell them to do, right when I tell them to do it. It really is strictly just a... a hiccup in the listening department, if that makes sense. Nothing physical at all.\n\nDoctor: Have you felt down, sad, or hopeless about these episodes, or have they affected your mood or enjoyment in activities you used to like?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, I wouldn't go that far. Hopeless is a very strong word, don't you think? I mean, I watch the evening news, and you see people who are truly hopeless, going through just awful, terrible things in the world. But me? No, no. I drive myself everywhere, take the same route down Elm Street to get to the museum, never get turned around or anything like that. I always know exactly what day it is, mostly because I keep a very strict routine since I retired from the workforce. Tuesday is trash day, Thursday is my morning shift at the information desk, Sunday is church... so I'm very anchored, you might say. \n\nIt’s really just that specific thing where I'm listening to someone and the words just sort of... evaporate while they're speaking. But once I actually catch what they're saying, or if I read it on a piece of paper, I remember it just fine! So, no, no confusion or real memory loss, just that frustrating tuning-out business when people are talking to me.\n\nDoctor: When you find yourself tuning out during conversations, are you aware of anything else going on in your mind or around you at that moment, like distractions or sudden thoughts pulling your attention away?\n\nPatient: You know, that’s the strangest part of the whole thing, it really is. If I were sitting there daydreaming about what I was going to have for lunch—which, by the way, I usually just have a simple turkey sandwich, nothing fancy, maybe a little bit of that spicy mustard my daughter brought me from her trip to upstate New York last fall—but if I was thinking about that, well, then it would make sense, wouldn't it? I’d say, 'Oh, I missed what you said because I was distracted by my stomach rumbling.' Or if there was a loud noise, like a siren going by outside the museum. We do get a fair amount of ambulances going down Elm Street because the county hospital is just two miles north of us, so you hear them quite a bit. \n\nBut no, it’s not like that at all. I’m not thinking about my grocery list, I’m not looking over the person's shoulder at a painting, I'm not distracted by anything I can actually put my finger on. It’s more like... well, it’s like my brain just goes to static. Just completely empty. \n\nOne second I'm listening to our coordinator, Susan—she's a lovely woman, been running the volunteer program for about ten years now, always wears these very colorful scarves—one second I'm listening to her talk about the new impressionist exhibit we're getting, and the next second, I realize I haven't processed a single word she said for a whole minute. And I try to search my brain, you know, to figure out where I went, what I was thinking about instead, and there's just nothing there. No sudden thoughts pulling me away, no distractions, just a big blank space where her words were supposed to go. It’s incredibly frustrating because if I knew what was distracting me, maybe I could fix it, you know? I could tell myself to stop thinking about the lawn or the groceries. But how do you stop yourself from thinking about absolutely nothing at all?\n\nDoctor: During these moments when your brain feels like it goes to static, do you lose awareness of what’s happening around you, or do you remain aware but just unable to process the words?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, no, I’m definitely still right there in the room. I haven't gone anywhere, so to speak. I know exactly where I am and what's going on around me. \n\nLike with Susan, for example, when she’s talking to me and my brain does that little static thing, I can still see her perfectly fine. I can see her waving her hands—she talks with her hands a lot, you see. Her husband is Italian, lovely man named Marco, makes a fantastic lasagna, and she always jokes that she picked up the hand-waving habit from his side of the family. So I can see her doing that, and I can feel the hard floor under my shoes. We have these beautiful polished marble floors in the main lobby of the museum, gorgeous to look at but very, very hard on the knees and lower back if you stand on them too long. That's actually why I had to go and buy these special orthopedic inserts from the pharmacy down on 4th street. They have the little gel pads in the heels? Highly recommend them, by the way, if you're on your feet all day in the clinic here. \n\nBut anyway, my point is, I can feel my feet on the floor, I can see the dust motes catching the light from the big bay windows, I can hear the hum of the air conditioner kicking on. I am completely, one hundred percent aware of my surroundings. It’s not like I pass out or fall asleep with my eyes open or anything scary like that. I read an article in a magazine once about people who have these little... I don't know, mini-seizures or something, where they just completely blank out and don't even know time passed. It's definitely not that. I know time is passing. \n\nI know I'm standing there, and I know she's talking to me. I can even hear the actual sound of her voice making noise. It's just... the meaning of the words just doesn't connect in my head. It's like she suddenly switched to speaking Greek halfway through the sentence. I’m just standing there, looking right at her, nodding my head like a fool, fully aware that I am nodding and fully aware that she is speaking, but the actual content? The instructions about the painting or the schedule? Just gone. Just noise. And I'm just waiting for her to finish her sentence so I can do the whole, \"I'm so sorry, my mind wandered, could you repeat that?\" routine. Which, like I said, is just getting so incredibly old. Because I am right there, I really am, the words just aren't clicking.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced any loss of awareness, jerking movements, or difficulty moving parts of your body during or right after these episodes?\n\nPatient: Oh, heavens no. Like I was just saying, the awareness is completely intact, I'm fully present the whole time. And as for jerking around or not being able to move my body? No, absolutely not. My body works just fine—well, you know, as fine as you can expect for a sixty-three-year-old! I mean, sure, I get a little stiffness in my left knee when the weather turns cold. We had a bit of a frost last week, and boy, did I feel it when I was trying to get down to pull some weeds around the mailbox. If I'm standing at the information desk handing out museum maps, my hand doesn't shake, I don't drop the pamphlets, I don't spill my coffee. I'm just... doing whatever I was already doing. I don't freeze up like a statue where I can't move my legs, either. I can walk, I can turn my head, I can shift my weight from one foot to the other without any trouble at all. \n\nI actually know a fellow, Richard, from my old bowling league—I don't bowl anymore because of my shoulder, but I still go down to the alley on Wednesdays to keep score and socialize, they serve a surprisingly good chili dog there—anyway, Richard had a mild stroke a few years back, and he said his arm just stopped working out of nowhere. Just hung there like a wet noodle. It was terrifying for him, just awful. But I don't experience anything even remotely close to that. My arms and legs do exactly what I tell them to do, right when I tell them to do it. It really is strictly just a... a hiccup in the listening department, if that makes sense. Nothing physical at all.\n\nDoctor: Have you felt down, sad, or hopeless about these episodes, or have they affected your mood or enjoyment in activities you used to like?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, I wouldn't go that far. Hopeless is a very strong word, don't you think? I mean, I watch the evening news, and you see people who are truly hopeless, going through just awful, terrible things in the world. But me? No, no. I'm just a bit aggravated with myself, that's all. It certainly hasn't ruined my mood or stopped me from enjoying my days. \n\nI still get up every morning at 6:30 sharp—well, sometimes 6:45 if the cat is sleeping on my feet. We have this big orange tabby named Marmalade, my daughter found him under a porch about five years ago, and he just insists on sleeping right across my ankles, making it nearly impossible to get out of bed without waking him. Just last week, we had a group of third graders come through from the local elementary school for a field trip, and seeing their little faces light up when they saw the dinosaur exhibit... well, they're not real bones, of course, they're plaster casts, but the kids don't care. Seeing that just fills me with absolute joy. And I still go to the bowling alley every Wednesday for my chili dog and to keep score for Richard and the rest of the guys. I haven't lost one single bit of enjoyment in any of the things I like to do. \n\nIt's really just... well, it's just an annoyance, truthfully. Like a leaky faucet in the guest bathroom. You don't get depressed over a leaky faucet, you don't sit around crying about it, you just want to figure out how to tighten the bolt so it stops dripping, if that makes sense. Just wanting to get the plumbing fixed, so to speak!\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any trouble focusing or keeping your attention on tasks like reading a book, watching TV, or doing puzzles, where you need to stay focused for a while?\n\nPatient: Well, now that you mention it, reading can be a bit of a chore sometimes. It's funny you bring that up, because I was just dealing with this the other day. \n\nSusan—the one I mentioned earlier, from the museum—she prints out these informational packets for us volunteers every time a new exhibit rotates in. They're usually, oh, I don't know, maybe ten or twelve pages long, stapled in the top left corner. She uses this very nice, heavy stock paper, but she insists on using a font that I swear is a size ten. I've told her, 'Susan, we're not spring chickens here, maybe bump it up to a twelve,' but she says it saves on the museum's printing budget, which I suppose I understand. \n\nBut anyway, I'll sit down in my armchair at home—the green one by the front window, it gets the absolute best light in the late afternoons—with one of these gallery packets or a set of notes she's given us. And I start out just fine. I really do. I read the first paragraph, maybe the second, and I'm taking it all in, learning about the Bronze Age or whatever it happens to be that month. \n\nBut then, after just a few minutes... it's the strangest thing. My eyes are still moving over the page, going line by line, left to right, just like they're supposed to. But my mind? It has completely wandered off. I'll be looking right at the words, but my brain is suddenly miles away, thinking about what I'm going to make for dinner, or wondering if I remembered to put the recycling bin out on the curb—pickup is Thursday mornings, you see, and the truck comes awfully early, usually right when I'm pouring my coffee. \n\nAnd then I'll suddenly realize I'm at the bottom of the page, and I haven't absorbed a single piece of information from the last three paragraphs. It's just like the listening thing, but with reading! My eyes did the work, but nobody was home to receive the mail, so to speak. So I have to go back up and read the exact same part all over again. Though, honestly, even with the crosswords, I'll stare at a clue for a 'five-letter word for boat' and the next thing I know I'm daydreaming about a fishing trip I took to Lake Michigan back in nineteen ninety-eight. Beautiful lake, by the way, though the wind coming off it will chill you right to the bone. But yes, I suppose keeping my attention locked on one thing for a long stretch, like a book or those gallery notes, is definitely a bit of a struggle.\n\nDoctor: When you're trying to focus on something like reading or doing a puzzle, do you find yourself getting distracted easily or losing track of what you're doing, even if there’s no obvious interruption?\n\nPatient: Well, I'm not really sure I'd use the word \"distracted,\" to be honest with you. When you say distracted, I always think of, oh, you know, someone trying to read a book while there's a marching band going by outside, or the telephone ringing off the hook, or kids running through the house screaming. None at all. It's just me and Marmalade. And Marmalade sleeps eighteen hours a day, usually right on top of my favorite embroidered throw pillow on the sofa. He'd say, \"Don't worry, I've got the important bits right here.\" But taking it all on by myself these last two years and four months... that's when it became glaringly obvious that my brain was taking these little detours. When you say strange or unwanted thoughts, I think of, oh, I don't know, those science fiction programs or something terribly dramatic. No, my thoughts are completely ordinary. Thoughts I can't get out of my head? Oh, goodness no. If anything, my problem is the exact opposite! I can't seem to *keep* a thought in my head half the time, let alone get one stuck there. My mind is more like a sieve than a steel trap, to be perfectly honest with you. 

I mean, sure, maybe I'll get a catchy jingle from a television commercial bouncing around in there for an hour or two—like that one for the local carpet cleaning service, the one with the little animated mop, they play it constantly during the evening news and it is just dreadfully repetitive—but that's just a minor nuisance. It's not something I'm trying desperately to stop thinking about, and it always just fades away on its own once I start doing something else. 

But as for real thoughts, or worries, getting trapped in my head? No, never. They just drift right on by. Like I was saying before, my thoughts are always moving from one thing to the next, like a bee in a flower garden. Just yesterday, I was in the kitchen trying to remember if I needed to buy more of those specific little garbage bags for the bathroom bin—the ones with the lavender scent that my sister Brenda insists I use—and before I could even open the cabinet to check under the sink, I saw a cardinal out the window at the bird feeder. 

Well, then I started wondering if the squirrels had gotten into the suet again, because they are just relentless this time of year, absolutely relentless! They actually figured out how to unlatch the supposedly "squirrel-proof" cage I bought at the hardware store, which wasn't cheap, let me tell you. So I went out to the yard to check the feeder, and by the time I came back inside, the thought about the garbage bags was long gone. Completely vanished! I didn't remember them again until I was already at the grocery store checkout. 

So no, I never have thoughts that get stuck or that I can't get rid of, no matter how hard I try. My thoughts just don't stick around long enough to overstay their welcome!

I hear the beginning, I hear the end, but the middle is just gone. \n\nAnd it’s so embarrassing, it really is, because I’m standing right there, looking right into their eyes, and I have to stop them and ask them to run it by me again. And I hate doing that. I really do. It makes me feel like I’m being rude or like I don't care about what they have to say, which isn't true at all! I want to hear them, I just... the words just slip right past me even when I'm staring right at their face. I just don't understand why I can't seem to hold onto a simple conversation without needing a rewind, and it's happening enough now that I'm just getting frustrated with myself.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any other changes in your thinking or memory lately, like forgetting things more often or feeling confused about time or places?\n\nPatient: Well, you know, I’ve actually asked myself that very same question. When you get to be my age—I'm 63, you know—you start to wonder if maybe the old memory bank is starting to rust a little bit. You hear stories about folks getting confused or forgetting their own phone numbers, or getting lost on their own street, and it terrifies you, it really does. But honestly? No. I haven’t noticed anything like that at all. My memory itself seems to be as sharp as a tack, thank goodness. \n\nFor instance, I can tell you the exact dates of every rotating exhibit we've had at the museum for the last three years, and I know all the names of the regular patrons who come in on Thursday mornings. Just this past weekend, I was telling my neighbor, Bill—he lives two doors down, got this beautiful golden retriever that always digs up my petunias, but that's a whole other story—anyway, I was telling him about a documentary I watched on the History Channel, and I remembered all the dates and the historical figures without missing a beat. So the information is definitely staying in my head once it actually gets in there! \n\nAnd as for getting confused about time or places, no, definitely not. I drive myself everywhere, take the same route down Elm Street to get to the museum, never get turned around or anything like that. I always know exactly what day it is, mostly because I keep a very strict routine since I retired from the workforce. Tuesday is trash day, Thursday is my morning shift at the information desk, Sunday is church... so I'm very anchored, you might say. \n\nIt’s really just that specific thing where I'm listening to someone and the words just sort of... evaporate while they're speaking. But once I actually catch what they're saying, or if I read it on a piece of paper, I remember it just fine! So, no, no confusion or real memory loss, just that frustrating tuning-out business when people are talking to me.\n\nDoctor: When you find yourself tuning out during conversations, are you aware of anything else going on in your mind or around you at that moment, like distractions or sudden thoughts pulling your attention away?\n\nPatient: You know, that’s the strangest part of the whole thing, it really is. If I were sitting there daydreaming about what I was going to have for lunch—which, by the way, I usually just have a simple turkey sandwich, nothing fancy, maybe a little bit of that spicy mustard my daughter brought me from her trip to upstate New York last fall—but if I was thinking about that, well, then it would make sense, wouldn't it? I’d say, 'Oh, I missed what you said because I was distracted by my stomach rumbling.' Or if there was a loud noise, like a siren going by outside the museum. We do get a fair amount of ambulances going down Elm Street because the county hospital is just two miles north of us, so you hear them quite a bit. \n\nBut no, it’s not like that at all. I’m not thinking about my grocery list, I’m not looking over the person's shoulder at a painting, I'm not distracted by anything I can actually put my finger on. It’s more like... well, it’s like my brain just goes to static. Just completely empty. \n\nOne second I'm listening to our coordinator, Susan—she's a lovely woman, been running the volunteer program for about ten years now, always wears these very colorful scarves—one second I'm listening to her talk about the new impressionist exhibit we're getting, and the next second, I realize I haven't processed a single word she said for a whole minute. And I try to search my brain, you know, to figure out where I went, what I was thinking about instead, and there's just nothing there. No sudden thoughts pulling me away, no distractions, just a big blank space where her words were supposed to go. It’s incredibly frustrating because if I knew what was distracting me, maybe I could fix it, you know? I could tell myself to stop thinking about the lawn or the groceries. But how do you stop yourself from thinking about absolutely nothing at all?\n\nDoctor: During these moments when your brain feels like it goes to static, do you lose awareness of what’s happening around you, or do you remain aware but just unable to process the words?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, no, I’m definitely still right there in the room. I haven't gone anywhere, so to speak. I know exactly where I am and what's going on around me. \n\nLike with Susan, for example, when she’s talking to me and my brain does that little static thing, I can still see her perfectly fine. I can see her waving her hands—she talks with her hands a lot, you see. Her husband is Italian, lovely man named Marco, makes a fantastic lasagna, and she always jokes that she picked up the hand-waving habit from his side of the family. So I can see her doing that, and I can feel the hard floor under my shoes. We have these beautiful polished marble floors in the main lobby of the museum, gorgeous to look at but very, very hard on the knees and lower back if you stand on them too long. That's actually why I had to go and buy these special orthopedic inserts from the pharmacy down on 4th street. They have the little gel pads in the heels? Highly recommend them, by the way, if you're on your feet all day in the clinic here. \n\nBut anyway, my point is, I can feel my feet on the floor, I can see the dust motes catching the light from the big bay windows, I can hear the hum of the air conditioner kicking on. I am completely, one hundred percent aware of my surroundings. It’s not like I pass out or fall asleep with my eyes open or anything scary like that. I read an article in a magazine once about people who have these little... I don't know, mini-seizures or something, where they just completely blank out and don't even know time passed. It's definitely not that. I know time is passing. \n\nI know I'm standing there, and I know she's talking to me. I can even hear the actual sound of her voice making noise. It's just... the meaning of the words just doesn't connect in my head. It's like she suddenly switched to speaking Greek halfway through the sentence. I’m just standing there, looking right at her, nodding my head like a fool, fully aware that I am nodding and fully aware that she is speaking, but the actual content? The instructions about the painting or the schedule? Just gone. Just noise. And I'm just waiting for her to finish her sentence so I can do the whole, \"I'm so sorry, my mind wandered, could you repeat that?\" routine. Which, like I said, is just getting so incredibly old. Because I am right there, I really am, the words just aren't clicking.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced any loss of awareness, jerking movements, or difficulty moving parts of your body during or right after these episodes?\n\nPatient: Oh, heavens no. Like I was just saying, the awareness is completely intact, I'm fully present the whole time. And as for jerking around or not being able to move my body? No, absolutely not. My body works just fine—well, you know, as fine as you can expect for a sixty-three-year-old! I mean, sure, I get a little stiffness in my left knee when the weather turns cold. We had a bit of a frost last week, and boy, did I feel it when I was trying to get down to pull some weeds around the mailbox. But that's just regular wear and tear, nothing to do with these little episodes. \n\nWhen my brain does that static thing, I don't twitch or jerk or anything like that. If I'm standing at the information desk handing out museum maps, my hand doesn't shake, I don't drop the pamphlets, I don't spill my coffee. I'm just... doing whatever I was already doing. I don't freeze up like a statue where I can't move my legs, either. I can walk, I can turn my head, I can shift my weight from one foot to the other without any trouble at all. \n\nI actually know a fellow, Richard, from my old bowling league—I don't bowl anymore because of my shoulder, but I still go down to the alley on Wednesdays to keep score and socialize, they serve a surprisingly good chili dog there—anyway, Richard had a mild stroke a few years back, and he said his arm just stopped working out of nowhere. Just hung there like a wet noodle. It was terrifying for him, just awful. But I don't experience anything even remotely close to that. My arms and legs do exactly what I tell them to do, right when I tell them to do it. It really is strictly just a... a hiccup in the listening department, if that makes sense. Nothing physical at all.\n\nDoctor: Have you felt down, sad, or hopeless about these episodes, or have they affected your mood or enjoyment in activities you used to like?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, I wouldn't go that far. Hopeless is a very strong word, don't you think? I mean, I watch the evening news, and you see people who are truly hopeless, going through just awful, terrible things in the world. But me? No, no. I'm just a bit aggravated with myself, that's all. It certainly hasn't ruined my mood or stopped me from enjoying my days. \n\nI still get up every morning at 6:30 sharp—well, sometimes 6:45 if the cat is sleeping on my feet. We have this big orange tabby named Marmalade, my daughter found him under a porch about five years ago, and he just insists on sleeping right across my ankles, making it nearly impossible to get out of bed without waking him. But anyway, I get up, I have my coffee—black, no sugar, doctor's orders for the blood sugar, you know—and I am just as happy as a clam to start my day. \n\nI still absolutely love going to the museum. Even with these little listening hiccups, I wouldn't trade my volunteer hours for the world. Just last week, we had a group of third graders come through from the local elementary school for a field trip, and seeing their little faces light up when they saw the dinosaur exhibit... well, they're not real bones, of course, they're plaster casts, but the kids don't care. Seeing that just fills me with absolute joy. And I still go to the bowling alley every Wednesday for my chili dog and to keep score for Richard and the rest of the guys. I haven't lost one single bit of enjoyment in any of the things I like to do. \n\nIt's really just... well, it's just an annoyance, truthfully. Like a leaky faucet in the guest bathroom. You don't get depressed over a leaky faucet, you don't sit around crying about it, you just want to figure out how to tighten the bolt so it stops dripping, if that makes sense. So no, no sadness or feeling down. Just wanting to get the plumbing fixed, so to speak!\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any trouble focusing or keeping your attention on tasks like reading a book, watching TV, or doing puzzles, where you need to stay focused for a while?\n\nPatient: Well, now that you mention it, reading can be a bit of a chore sometimes. It's funny you bring that up, because I was just dealing with this the other day. \n\nSusan—the one I mentioned earlier, from the museum—she prints out these informational packets for us volunteers every time a new exhibit rotates in. They're usually, oh, I don't know, maybe ten or twelve pages long, stapled in the top left corner. She uses this very nice, heavy stock paper, but she insists on using a font that I swear is a size ten. I've told her, 'Susan, we're not spring chickens here, maybe bump it up to a twelve,' but she says it saves on the museum's printing budget, which I suppose I understand. \n\nBut anyway, I'll sit down in my armchair at home—the green one by the front window, it gets the absolute best light in the late afternoons—with one of these gallery packets or a set of notes she's given us. And I start out just fine. I really do. I read the first paragraph, maybe the second, and I'm taking it all in, learning about the Bronze Age or whatever it happens to be that month. \n\nBut then, after just a few minutes... it's the strangest thing. My eyes are still moving over the page, going line by line, left to right, just like they're supposed to. But my mind? It has completely wandered off. I'll be looking right at the words, but my brain is suddenly miles away, thinking about what I'm going to make for dinner, or wondering if I remembered to put the recycling bin out on the curb—pickup is Thursday mornings, you see, and the truck comes awfully early, usually right when I'm pouring my coffee. \n\nAnd then I'll suddenly realize I'm at the bottom of the page, and I haven't absorbed a single piece of information from the last three paragraphs. It's just like the listening thing, but with reading! My eyes did the work, but nobody was home to receive the mail, so to speak. So I have to go back up and read the exact same part all over again. Sometimes I have to read the same paragraph three or four times before it actually sticks in my head. \n\nAs for television, well, I watch my evening news, like I said, and maybe a documentary here and there on the history channel, but I usually end up fiddling with a crossword puzzle while it's on because I just can't just sit and stare at the screen. Though, honestly, even with the crosswords, I'll stare at a clue for a 'five-letter word for boat' and the next thing I know I'm daydreaming about a fishing trip I took to Lake Michigan back in nineteen ninety-eight. Beautiful lake, by the way, though the wind coming off it will chill you right to the bone. But yes, I suppose keeping my attention locked on one thing for a long stretch, like a book or those gallery notes, is definitely a bit of a struggle.\n\nDoctor: When you're trying to focus on something like reading or doing a puzzle, do you find yourself getting distracted easily or losing track of what you're doing, even if there’s no obvious interruption?\n\nPatient: Well, I'm not really sure I'd use the word \"distracted,\" to be honest with you. When you say distracted, I always think of, oh, you know, someone trying to read a book while there's a marching band going by outside, or the telephone ringing off the hook, or kids running through the house screaming. But my house is quiet as a mouse. \n\nI live on a cul-de-sac, you see, over on Elm Street—been there since nineteen eighty-two, back when they first built the subdivision. It's a wonderful neighborhood, very peaceful. Most of the original owners have moved on or passed away, God rest their souls, but it's stayed very quiet. The absolute most noise we get is when Mr. Henderson two doors down decides to use his gas-powered leaf blower on a Saturday morning. None at all. It's just me and Marmalade. And Marmalade sleeps eighteen hours a day, usually right on top of my favorite embroidered throw pillow on the sofa. I mean, if I'm sitting there with Susan's museum packet, I know exactly what I'm doing. It's really just the daydreaming while the house is perfectly quiet, just like I was saying.\n\nDoctor: Have these episodes of your mind going blank come on suddenly, or have they been getting worse gradually over time?\n\nPatient: Well, it wasn't exactly a sudden overnight thing, like waking up with a sore throat or a stiff neck, but I can tell you exactly when it really started becoming a noticeable issue. It’s been right about two years and four months now. I know the timeline so specifically because, well... it was right after my dear friend Arthur passed away. \n\nArthur and I, we were quite the pair at the museum. We started volunteering there together back in... oh, it must have been two thousand and fifteen, maybe sixteen. He was such a wonderful fellow, always had a joke ready for the security guards, always wore these brightly colored bowties. But he had a bad heart, you see, and he passed away quite suddenly. He handled all the important paperwork, the scheduling with the local schools, making sure everyone had their gallery packets and knew where they were supposed to stand when the big tours came through. He kept everything perfectly organized in this giant red binder he carried around. But when he died, well, there was a big gap, and Susan asked me to step up. So I took over the museum liaison duties all by myself. And let me tell you, it is a tremendous amount of responsibility for one person to manage! \n\nAnd that is exactly when this whole... mind going blank business really started causing trouble for me. Because suddenly, I didn't have Arthur there to tap me on the shoulder if I spaced out during a meeting, and I had to read every single page of those informational packets myself to prepare the other volunteers. Before he passed, if my mind took a little walk while we were reading up on the new exhibits, Arthur would just fill me in on whatever I missed. He'd say, \"Don't worry, I've got the important bits right here.\" But taking it all on by myself these last two years and four months... that's when it became glaringly obvious that my brain was taking these little detours. So I suppose my mind might have always wandered a little bit, but the trouble of it—the real, noticeable trouble—started exactly when I had to take over for Arthur.\n\nDoctor: During the times when your mind goes blank, do you ever experience any strange or unwanted thoughts, mental images, or a sense that things are not real?\n\nPatient: Oh, heavens no, nothing like that. When you say strange or unwanted thoughts, I think of, oh, I don't know, those science fiction programs or something terribly dramatic. No, my thoughts are completely ordinary. Almost painfully boring, if I'm being entirely honest with you! \n\nWhen my mind takes its little walks, it's always to very everyday, mundane places. Like I mentioned before, it's the recycling, or what I'm having for supper. She’s gotten terribly picky in her old age, you see. And wouldn't you know it, the grocery store over on Main Street just rearranged their aisles last month, so the cat food is completely on the other side of the store now, right next to the baking supplies, which makes no sense at all to me. \n\nSo, no, there are no strange mental images or anything unwanted. Oh, no, nothing like that. If I'm up and moving, or doing my hobbies, I have all the drive in the world. It's really just the sitting still and staring at the dry paperwork that trips me up, never the actual doing of the things I love.\n\nDoctor: During the times when your mind seems to wander or go blank, do you ever lose track of what’s happening around you—like not knowing where you are, who you're with, or what you were doing—until someone snaps you out of it?\n\nPatient: Oh, heavens, no, nothing frightening like that! She's always worrying about my memory, you see, always asking if I'm doing my crossword puzzles to keep my mind sharp. But my memory is absolutely fine. I might sit there staring at the exact same picture of the mayor for five minutes without absorbing a thing! It's really just the focusing on the dry, boring bits of paper that gets me into trouble, not any sort of lack of joy or anything gloomy like that.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever find yourself not wanting to get involved in activities, even the ones you usually enjoy, or feeling like it's just too much effort to do the things you used to do with ease?\n\nPatient: Oh, my, no. Not in the slightest. If anything, I probably try to get involved in *too* many things, if you were to ask my sister, Brenda. She's always calling on the telephone telling me I need to slow down and act my age, whatever that means! \n\nBut no, I never feel like my activities are too much effort. Like I was just saying about the museum, I am always eager to get down there. In fact, just last weekend Susan called me up and asked if anyone could come in on a Saturday—which isn't my usual day, as you know, I'm strictly Tuesdays and Thursdays—but she needed help setting up the folding chairs for a special visiting lecturer. It was some fellow from the state university coming to talk about 19th-century agricultural tools. Now, maybe not the most thrilling topic in the world, between you and me, but I didn't hesitate for a single second. I was right out of my green armchair, had my coat on, and drove straight down there. \n\nIt took us nearly three hours to get all those metal chairs arranged just right in the main hall, mostly because Susan is incredibly particular about the aisles being exactly thirty-six inches wide for the fire code. She actually brought a tape measure out of her desk! But did it feel like too much effort for me? Not a bit! I actually quite enjoyed it. It gets the blood pumping, you know? Now, I will admit my knees felt it the next morning, they aren't quite what they were when I was working, so I did have to take a little breather halfway through the setup and have a cup of that hazelnut coffee in the breakroom. But the *desire* to do it, the motivation, was absolutely there. \n\nI never wake up and think, \"Oh, I just can't be bothered today.\" I just don't have it in me to sit around doing nothing. Even with Marmalade, when she decides she wants to play at five o'clock in the morning and brings her little felt toy mouse—the one with the bell on the tail—right into my bedroom, I never just ignore her or feel like it's too much work. I might groan a little bit about the hour, naturally, but I'll sit up in bed and toss that mouse across the rug for her until she's finally tired herself out. \n\nSo no, I don't have any trouble at all wanting to do things, or feeling like it's all too much work. If I'm up and moving, or doing my hobbies, I have all the drive in the world. It's really just the sitting still and staring at the dry paperwork that trips me up, never the actual doing of the things I love.\n\nDoctor: During the times when your mind seems to wander or go blank, do you ever lose track of what’s happening around you—like not knowing where you are, who you're with, or what you were doing—until someone snaps you out of it?\n\nPatient: Oh, heavens, no, nothing frightening like that! I mean, if I started forgetting where I was or who I was sitting with, well, my sister Brenda would probably have me packed off to an assisted living facility before I could even blink. She's always worrying about my memory, you see, always asking if I'm doing my crossword puzzles to keep my mind sharp. But my memory is absolutely fine. It’s just my attention that takes a little stroll.\n\nWhen my mind wanders, I know exactly where I am the entire time. If I'm at home, I know I’m right there in my green armchair. I know I'm in my own living room, I know Marmalade is asleep on the rug—usually right on top of the heating vent, she absolutely loves that spot in the winter, even though I always worry she's going to singe her fur one of these days. I'm completely aware of the room. \n\nAnd if I'm at the museum, and Susan is talking to me... well, I might not process a single word she just said about, oh, say, the new exhibit on the local textile mills, because I was busy wondering if I remembered to take the chicken out of the freezer for dinner. But I still know I'm at the museum! I still know it's Susan standing right in front of me in her blue cardigan. It’s not like I snap out of a trance and wonder, \"Who are you and how did I get here?\" \n\nIt's really just... I lose the thread of the conversation, or the paragraph I'm trying to read. I know exactly what I *was* supposed to be doing, I just sort of... stopped focusing on it for a minute to think about something else entirely. So no, I never lose track of my surroundings or the people I'm with. I'm completely aware of the world around me. It's just the task right in front of my nose that gets a bit fuzzy!\n\nDoctor: When you realize your mind has wandered during reading or conversations, do you feel like you have to work especially hard to bring your attention back, or does it come back easily when you notice it’s drifted?\n\nPatient: Well, you know, once I actually realize I’ve drifted off, it’s really no trouble at all to get back on track. Like I was saying, I read the physical paper every morning in my green armchair. Let's say I'm reading an article about the town council—they've been going on and on for weeks in the local section about the zoning permits for that new strip mall over on Route 7, which, frankly, is going to make the traffic just absolutely unbearable during the evening rush, they never think these things through—and right in the middle of a paragraph, my mind just decides to wander off. I'll start wondering if I bought enough of Marmalade's salmon paté at the grocery store on Tuesday, or if I need to make a special trip to the pet shop. \n\nNow, the tricky part is just *noticing* that I've stopped reading. I might sit there staring at the exact same picture of the mayor for five minutes without absorbing a thing! But the very second I think to myself, \"Oh, goodness, I'm not reading a word of this,\" I just blink, look down at the page, and I'm right back in it. I just find the last sentence I actually remember and off I go again. It doesn't take any special effort.\n\nIt’s the exact same thing when I'm talking to Susan at the museum. If she's telling me about the new schedule for the third-grade school tours, and I start thinking about whether I remembered to leave the porch light on for the mail carrier... well, the moment I realize I've tuned her out, I just say, \"Oh, I'm so sorry Susan, my mind took a little detour there, what was that last part?\" And I'm instantly right back in the conversation with her. \n\nIt never feels like hard work. It's not like trying to push a heavy wheelbarrow up a steep hill—which I actually did try to do last spring when I was helping Mr. Henderson with his garden mulch, because his grandson was supposed to come help but never showed up, and let me tell you, my lower back was complaining about that for a solid week, I had to use the heating pad every single night while I watched Jeopardy. But no, pulling my attention back isn't like heavy lifting at all. It just pops right back to the present the moment I realize it went missing in the first place.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had periods in the past where you felt persistently down, lost interest in things, or had trouble enjoying activities, even if they didn't last very long?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, I can't say I have. She had this whole theory because her husband, my brother-in-law Gary, well, when he retired from the post office he just sat in his recliner for six months and watched golf until he drove her half mad. She thought I'd do the exact same thing, just lose all my drive and get down in the dumps. \n\nBut I just never felt that way. Not even for a short spell. I always have something I want to do, and I always enjoy doing it. I'll just turn on all the lamps in the living room, put the kettle on for tea or maybe make a cup of that hazelnut coffee, get Marmalade settled on her heating vent, and I'm perfectly content. \n\nI never lose my interest in my hobbies or the museum or anything like that. I mean, sure, I might get a little frustrated if I drop a tiny screw while I'm trying to fix the toaster and it rolls under the refrigerator, but that's just being annoyed, that's not feeling down or depressed. I might get distracted from my activities, like we were talking about earlier with the newspaper, but the actual enjoyment of them? The spark? No, that's always there. I've just never been the sort to get a dark cloud over my head or lose my taste for the things I love.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had thoughts that you couldn't get out of your head, even if you tried not to think about them?\n\nPatient: Thoughts I can't get out of my head? Oh, goodness no. If anything, my problem is the exact opposite! I can't seem to *keep* a thought in my head half the time, let alone get one stuck there. It's not something I'm trying desperately to stop thinking about, and it always just fades away on its own once I start doing something else. \n\nBut as for real thoughts, or worries, getting trapped in my head? They actually figured out how to unlatch the supposedly \"squirrel-proof\" cage I bought at the hardware store, which wasn't cheap, let me tell you.
