So, no, no confusion or real memory loss, just that frustrating tuning-out business when people are talking to me.\n\nDoctor: When you find yourself tuning out during conversations, are you aware of anything else going on in your mind or around you at that moment, like distractions or sudden thoughts pulling your attention away?\n\nPatient: You know, that’s the strangest part of the whole thing, it really is. If I were sitting there daydreaming about what I was going to have for lunch—which, by the way, I usually just have a simple turkey sandwich, nothing fancy, maybe a little bit of that spicy mustard my daughter brought me from her trip to upstate New York last fall—but if I was thinking about that, well, then it would make sense, wouldn't it? I’d say, 'Oh, I missed what you said because I was distracted by my stomach rumbling.' Or if there was a loud noise, like a siren going by outside the museum. We do get a fair amount of ambulances going down Elm Street because the county hospital is just two miles north of us, so you hear them quite a bit. \n\nBut no, it’s not like that at all. I’m not thinking about my grocery list, I’m not looking over the person's shoulder at a painting, I'm not distracted by anything I can actually put my finger on. It’s more like... well, it’s like my brain just goes to static. Just completely empty. \n\nOne second I'm listening to our coordinator, Susan—she's a lovely woman, been running the volunteer program for about ten years now, always wears these very colorful scarves—one second I'm listening to her talk about the new impressionist exhibit we're getting, and the next second, I realize I haven't processed a single word she said for a whole minute. And I try to search my brain, you know, to figure out where I went, what I was thinking about instead, and there's just nothing there. No sudden thoughts pulling me away, no distractions, just a big blank space where her words were supposed to go. It’s incredibly frustrating because if I knew what was distracting me, maybe I could fix it, you know? I could tell myself to stop thinking about the lawn or the groceries. But how do you stop yourself from thinking about absolutely nothing at all?\n\nDoctor: During these moments when your brain feels like it goes to static, do you lose awareness of what’s happening around you, or do you remain aware but just unable to process the words?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, no, I’m definitely still right there in the room. I haven't gone anywhere, so to speak. I know exactly where I am and what's going on around me. \n\nLike with Susan, for example, when she’s talking to me and my brain does that little static thing, I can still see her perfectly fine. I can see her waving her hands—she talks with her hands a lot, you see. Her husband is Italian, lovely man named Marco, makes a fantastic lasagna, and she always jokes that she picked up the hand-waving habit from his side of the family. So I can see her doing that, and I can feel the hard floor under my shoes. We have these beautiful polished marble floors in the main lobby of the museum, gorgeous to look at but very, very hard on the knees and lower back if you stand on them too long. That's actually why I had to go and buy these special orthopedic inserts from the pharmacy down on 4th street. They have the little gel pads in the heels? Highly recommend them, by the way, if you're on your feet all day in the clinic here. \n\nBut anyway, my point is, I can feel my feet on the floor, I can see the dust motes catching the light from the big bay windows, I can hear the hum of the air conditioner kicking on. I am completely, one hundred percent aware of my surroundings. It’s not like I pass out or fall asleep with my eyes open or anything scary like that. I read an article in a magazine once about people who have these little... I don't know, mini-seizures or something, where they just completely blank out and don't even know time passed. It's definitely not that. I know time is passing. \n\nI know I'm standing there, and I know she's talking to me. I can even hear the actual sound of her voice making noise. It's just... the meaning of the words just doesn't connect in my head. It's like she suddenly switched to speaking Greek halfway through the sentence. I’m just standing there, looking right at her, nodding my head like a fool, fully aware that I am nodding and fully aware that she is speaking, but the actual content? The instructions about the painting or the schedule? Just gone. Just noise. And I'm just waiting for her to finish her sentence so I can do the whole, \"I'm so sorry, my mind wandered, could you repeat that?\" routine. Which, like I said, is just getting so incredibly old. Because I am right there, I really am, the words just aren't clicking.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced any loss of awareness, jerking movements, or difficulty moving parts of your body during or right after these episodes?\n\nPatient: Oh, heavens no. Like I was just saying, the awareness is completely intact, I'm fully present the whole time. And as for jerking around or not being able to move my body? No, absolutely not. My body works just fine—well, you know, as fine as you can expect for a sixty-three-year-old! I mean, sure, I get a little stiffness in my left knee when the weather turns cold. We had a bit of a frost last week, and boy, did I feel it when I was trying to get down to pull some weeds around the mailbox. But that's just regular wear and tear, nothing to do with these little episodes. \n\nWhen my brain does that static thing, I don't twitch or jerk or anything like that. If I'm standing at the information desk handing out museum maps, my hand doesn't shake, I don't drop the pamphlets, I don't spill my coffee. I'm just... doing whatever I was already doing. I don't freeze up like a statue where I can't move my legs, either. I can walk, I can turn my head, I can shift my weight from one foot to the other without any trouble at all. \n\nI actually know a fellow, Richard, from my old bowling league—I don't bowl anymore because of my shoulder, but I still go down to the alley on Wednesdays to keep score and socialize, they serve a surprisingly good chili dog there—anyway, Richard had a mild stroke a few years back, and he said his arm just stopped working out of nowhere. Just hung there like a wet noodle. It was terrifying for him, just awful. But I don't experience anything even remotely close to that. My arms and legs do exactly what I tell them to do, right when I tell them to do it. It really is strictly just a... a hiccup in the listening department, if that makes sense. Nothing physical at all.\n\nDoctor: Have you felt down, sad, or hopeless about these episodes, or have they affected your mood or enjoyment in activities you used to like?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, I wouldn't go that far. Hopeless is a very strong word, don't you think? I mean, I watch the evening news, and you see people who are truly hopeless, going through just awful, terrible things in the world. But me? No, no. I'm just a bit aggravated with myself, that's all. It certainly hasn't ruined my mood or stopped me from enjoying my days. \n\nI still get up every morning at 6:30 sharp—well, sometimes 6:45 if the cat is sleeping on my feet. We have this big orange tabby named Marmalade, my daughter found him under a porch about five years ago, and he just insists on sleeping right across my ankles, making it nearly impossible to get out of bed without waking him. But anyway, I get up, I have my coffee—black, no sugar, doctor's orders for the blood sugar, you know—and I am just as happy as a clam to start my day. \n\nI still absolutely love going to the museum. Even with these little listening hiccups, I wouldn't trade my volunteer hours for the world. Just last week, we had a group of third graders come through from the local elementary school for a field trip, and seeing their little faces light up when they saw the dinosaur exhibit... well, they're not real bones, of course, they're plaster casts, but the kids don't care. Seeing that just fills me with absolute joy. And I still go to the bowling alley every Wednesday for my chili dog and to keep score for Richard and the rest of the guys. I haven't lost one single bit of enjoyment in any of the things I like to do. \n\nIt's really just... well, it's just an annoyance, truthfully. Like a leaky faucet in the guest bathroom. You don't get depressed over a leaky faucet, you don't sit around crying about it, you just want to figure out how to tighten the bolt so it stops dripping, if that makes sense. So no, no sadness or feeling down. Just wanting to get the plumbing fixed, so to speak!\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any trouble focusing or keeping your attention on tasks like reading a book, watching TV, or doing puzzles, where you need to stay focused for a while?\n\nPatient: Well, now that you mention it, reading can be a bit of a chore sometimes. It's funny you bring that up, because I was just dealing with this the other day. \n\nSusan—the one I mentioned earlier, from the museum—she prints out these informational packets for us volunteers every time a new exhibit rotates in. They're usually, oh, I don't know, maybe ten or twelve pages long, stapled in the top left corner. She uses this very nice, heavy stock paper, but she insists on using a font that I swear is a size ten. I've told her, 'Susan, we're not spring chickens here, maybe bump it up to a twelve,' but she says it saves on the museum's printing budget, which I suppose I understand. \n\nBut anyway, I'll sit down in my armchair at home—the green one by the front window, it gets the absolute best light in the late afternoons—with one of these gallery packets or a set of notes she's given us. And I start out just fine. I really do. I read the first paragraph, maybe the second, and I'm taking it all in, learning about the Bronze Age or whatever it happens to be that month. \n\nBut then, after just a few minutes... it's the strangest thing. My eyes are still moving over the page, going line by line, left to right, just like they're supposed to. But my mind? It has completely wandered off. I'll be looking right at the words, but my brain is suddenly miles away, thinking about what I'm going to make for dinner, or wondering if I remembered to put the recycling bin out on the curb—pickup is Thursday mornings, you see, and the truck comes awfully early, usually right when I'm pouring my coffee. \n\nAnd then I'll suddenly realize I'm at the bottom of the page, and I haven't absorbed a single piece of information from the last three paragraphs. It's just like the listening thing, but with reading! My eyes did the work, but nobody was home to receive the mail, so to speak. So I have to go back up and read the exact same part all over again. Sometimes I have to read the same paragraph three or four times before it actually sticks in my head. \n\nAs for television, well, I watch my evening news, like I said, and maybe a documentary here and there on the history channel, but I usually end up fiddling with a crossword puzzle while it's on because I just can't just sit and stare at the screen. Though, honestly, even with the crosswords, I'll stare at a clue for a 'five-letter word for boat' and the next thing I know I'm daydreaming about a fishing trip I took to Lake Michigan back in nineteen ninety-eight. Beautiful lake, by the way, though the wind coming off it will chill you right to the bone. But yes, I suppose keeping my attention locked on one thing for a long stretch, like a book or those gallery notes, is definitely a bit of a struggle.\n\nDoctor: When you're trying to focus on something like reading or doing a puzzle, do you find yourself getting distracted easily or losing track of what you're doing, even if there’s no obvious interruption?\n\nPatient: Well, I'm not really sure I'd use the word \"distracted,\" to be honest with you. When you say distracted, I always think of, oh, you know, someone trying to read a book while there's a marching band going by outside, or the telephone ringing off the hook, or kids running through the house screaming. But my house is quiet as a mouse. \n\nI live on a cul-de-sac, you see, over on Elm Street—been there since nineteen eighty-two, back when they first built the subdivision. It's a wonderful neighborhood, very peaceful. Most of the original owners have moved on or passed away, God rest their souls, but it's stayed very quiet. And don't even get me started on that, he runs that thing for two solid hours just to move a handful of oak leaves from his driveway to the gutter! \n\nBut anyway, inside my house, there are no interruptions. None at all. It's just me and Marmalade. And Marmalade sleeps eighteen hours a day, usually right on top of my favorite embroidered throw pillow on the sofa. It's really just the daydreaming while the house is perfectly quiet, just like I was saying.\n\nDoctor: Have these episodes of your mind going blank come on suddenly, or have they been getting worse gradually over time?\n\nPatient: Well, it wasn't exactly a sudden overnight thing, like waking up with a sore throat or a stiff neck, but I can tell you exactly when it really started becoming a noticeable issue. We started volunteering there together back in... oh, it must have been two thousand and fifteen, maybe sixteen. He handled all the important paperwork, the scheduling with the local schools, making sure everyone had their gallery packets and knew where they were supposed to stand when the big tours came through. He kept everything perfectly organized in this giant red binder he carried around. But when he died, well, there was a big gap, and Susan asked me to step up. Because suddenly, I didn't have Arthur there to tap me on the shoulder if I spaced out during a meeting, and I had to read every single page of those informational packets myself to prepare the other volunteers. Before he passed, if my mind took a little walk while we were reading up on the new exhibits, Arthur would just fill me in on whatever I missed. He'd say, \"Don't worry, I've got the important bits right here.\" But taking it all on by myself these last two years and four months... that's when it became glaringly obvious that my brain was taking these little detours. So I suppose my mind might have always wandered a little bit, but the trouble of it—the real, noticeable trouble—started exactly when I had to take over for Arthur.\n\nDoctor: During the times when your mind goes blank, do you ever experience any strange or unwanted thoughts, mental images, or a sense that things are not real?\n\nPatient: Oh, heavens no, nothing like that. When you say strange or unwanted thoughts, I think of, oh, I don't know, those science fiction programs or something terribly dramatic. No, my thoughts are completely ordinary. Almost painfully boring, if I'm being entirely honest with you! \n\nWhen my mind takes its little walks, it's always to very everyday, mundane places. Like I mentioned before, it's the recycling, or what I'm having for supper. Just yesterday, for instance, I was supposed to be reading up on a new pottery exhibit—Mesopotamian, I believe, though don't quote me on that, Susan just handed us the packet on Tuesday—and my mind wandered right off to Marmalade's food situation. She’s gotten terribly picky in her old age, you see. She used to eat the dry kibble right out of the bag without a fuss, but now she turns her nose up at absolutely anything that isn't the salmon paté. And wouldn't you know it, the grocery store over on Main Street just rearranged their aisles last month, so the cat food is completely on the other side of the store now, right next to the baking supplies, which makes no sense at all to me. \n\nSo, no, there are no strange mental images or anything unwanted. Oh, no, nothing like that. My goodness, if I started getting dizzy every time my mind wandered off to the grocery store, I'd probably never be able to safely stand up from my chair! \n\nNow, since you mention changes in vision, I will say my eyesight isn't quite what it used to be when I was thirty, of course. If I'm up and moving, or doing my hobbies, I have all the drive in the world. It's really just the sitting still and staring at the dry paperwork that trips me up, never the actual doing of the things I love.\n\nDoctor: During the times when your mind seems to wander or go blank, do you ever lose track of what’s happening around you—like not knowing where you are, who you're with, or what you were doing—until someone snaps you out of it?\n\nPatient: Oh, heavens, no, nothing frightening like that! She's always worrying about my memory, you see, always asking if I'm doing my crossword puzzles to keep my mind sharp. But my memory is absolutely fine. If she's telling me about the new schedule for the third-grade school tours, and I start thinking about whether I remembered to leave the porch light on for the mail carrier... well, the moment I realize I've tuned her out, I just say, \"Oh, I'm so sorry Susan, my mind took a little detour there, what was that last part?\" And I'm instantly right back in the conversation with her. \n\nIt never feels like hard work. It just pops right back to the present the moment I realize it went missing in the first place.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had periods in the past where you felt persistently down, lost interest in things, or had trouble enjoying activities, even if they didn't last very long?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, I can't say I have. I don't suddenly forget I have a piece of paper in my hand or start doing something else entirely, like getting up to vacuum and leaving the book behind.
